claims.text: Eutectic high-entropy alloys consist of dual-phase lamellar colonies.
Internal boundaries in the lamellar colonies serve as microcrack-initiation sites during room-temperature tensile deformation.
A controlled sub-annealing heat treatment can trigger minor solute segregation at lamellar-colony boundaries.
Heat-treatment-induced segregation will form nanoscale ductile interfacial films at the boundaries.
The targeted interfacial film will be continuous or semi-continuous along internal lamellar-colony boundaries.
The interfacial films will fill microstructural discontinuities and improve bonding between lamellae.
The interfacial films will inhibit microcrack initiation.
The interfacial films will inhibit microcrack propagation.
The interfacial films will contribute to load transfer between lamellae.
The interfacial films will delay localized deformation.
The proposed mechanisms will simultaneously improve strength and room-temperature tensile ductility.
Annealed specimens will have higher yield strength than the as-solidified baseline.
Annealed specimens will have higher ultimate tensile strength than the as-solidified baseline.
Annealed specimens will have greater room-temperature tensile elongation than the as-solidified baseline.
Keeping the treatment below a suitable temperature-time limit can avoid excessive lamellar coarsening and deleterious-phase formation while still driving segregation.
The intervention will be effective only when interfacial films form without appreciable lamellar coarsening or formation of brittle phases.
The intervention's effectiveness may depend on alloy chemistry and the available processing window for controlled segregation.
